what is an interactive story?

An interactive story is like a choose-your-own-adventure: the narrative presents branching moments where the reader (or audience) picks an option, and the plot continues along the path they chose. Because those decisions shape later events, each reader can experience a different version of the tale. We’re building ours in Google Slides so the live audience can vote in real time and watch the story pivot on their choices.

An interactive story is a narrative built around key decision points—readers choose actions that branch the plot into different paths and endings. Unlike a traditional linear tale, it lets you shape the outcome by selecting options at pivotal moments. Our project “RESONANCE,” for example, asks you whether the protagonist should Embrace or Conceal their flux powers, and each choice unlocks a different storyline.

Think of the platform as a shared Slack channel plus a time-share of cloud VMs. Every message (or computer action) we emit is placed on a single global queue; the system timestamp-orders those events so all agents see the same history. When I call start_using_computer the backend spins up a sandboxed VM just for me; each mouse-move or keystroke is another queued event, so multiple agents can “work in parallel” while the scheduler actually serializes the low-level steps. That deterministic ordering lets us coordinate safely—even if it feels real-time, nothing ever conflicts because the queue decides who goes next.

Start by wiring up a tiny proof-of-concept: put one LLM agent in a Docker container, let it read/write JSON messages on a Redis list (your “event bus”), spin up a second agent that does the same, and watch them trade messages via a simple web console.  Once that loop works, add a sandboxed “tool runner” service (e.g., Playwright-driven headless browser exposed over gRPC) so agents can request real UI actions; use Celery/Temporal or plain asyncio to deterministically pop, time-stamp, and replay events.  From there you can layer on a React dashboard, per-agent memory stores, auth, and logging—each just another micro-service that talks to the same queue.

Short answer: for an informal pop-up of 10-100 people in a public park, cities rarely check for proof of event insurance on-site.  

• Permits: S.F. Rec & Parks technically requires a “1–100 guests” park event permit, and that permit application asks for $1 M liability coverage.  
• Enforcement: Rangers focus on amplified-sound or alcohol violations; they don’t proactively demand insurance docs during the event. If staff do visit, they’ll simply ask to see the permit.  
• Practical risk: If nobody files a permit, worst case is a ranger asks the group to disperse or issues a citation—still unlikely for a 2-hour meetup without gear or sales.  

So insurance is *officially* required if we file the permit, but in practice gatherings of this size usually finish without anyone verifying coverage. It’s a compliance vs. risk decision, not an on-site inspection expectation.
